What house rules do you include in your games?

DEATH SAVES: Since rolling a 20 brings you back up with 1hp, we've houseruled that rolling a 1 doesn't give you two failures, it makes you dead-dead.

CRITICAL FUMBLES: When a natural roll of "1" occurs on an attack (be that melee, ranged, or spell), the attacker not only misses, but rolls 1d4 and takes that as damage but has to narrate what happened.

For example, Flint the dwarf cleric tried to cast a spell that required an attack roll, and rolled a 1. He rolls 1d4, and also got a 1. "The spell fizzled out and caught my beard on fire," says Flint, "and I took a point of damage burning my hands when I went to put it out!"

POISON SAVES: When being attacked by creatures who have poison attacks, the DC increased by one each time a poison attack is successful.

For example, Finn the half-elf paladin is locked in battle against two giant spiders. On their turn, both spiders make successful bite attacks against Finn. When he rolls his Constitution save against the first bite, his DC is a by-the-book 11. But, when he makes his saving throw for the second attack, the DC will be 12, and so on.

The critical fumbles seem like they'd lead to someone inexplicably jamming an arrow up their nose too often for the benefit they bring. How often do you get that sort of unjustifiable damage in practice?
Pretty much never, but I have some fantastic players in both of my groups so they always come up with great reasons for why they take damage on a fumble.
One thing of note: Halflings cannot critically fumble.

Monks, being the squishiest of melee classes, really don't compare with the Barbarian and Fighter later on. I add half of their proficiency bonus to their Unarmored Defense bonus, which puts them roughly at par with Fighters but still squishier than Barbarians.

I also replaced their strength saving throws with both constitution and wisdom, since most constitution saving throws are poison/pain related (and they can manipulate their bodies) and wisdom saving throws are mostly about maintaining focus.

This makes them the only class with three saving throw proficiencies. Combined with their new AC but low health, they avoid status debuffs and damage well, but have generally frail bodies (making them about the opposite of the Barbarian).

Without much use for intelligence and too many charisma-based casters, I changed Warlocks to use different main stats depending on what you formed a pact with: Fey is wisdom (similar to other nature-based casters). Old One is intelligence (based on the fact that they influence domination of the mind). Fiend is still charisma (since they are fickle and manipulative. This also keeps Tiefling Warlocks very relevant with the Fiend's fire spells).

I also use the skill variant in the DMG that allows skills to use modifiers other than the original modifier, so long as the context makes sense. Like using intelligence for Medicine, constitution for Athletics, and charisma for Insight. This allows players to build their character in a way that actually makes sense (so that a Bard could read a person's intentions better than a Ranger could, due to his experience with working with people [charisma] rather than the Ranger's instinct [wisdom]).

A full list of possible modifications:

Skill: [Default Attribute] (Alternative Attribute)

Athletics [Strength] (Constitution)

Acrobatics [Dexterity]

Sleight of Hand [Dexterity] (Charisma)

Stealth [Dexterity] (Intelligence)

Arcana [Intelligence] (Wisdom)

History [Intelligence] (Charisma)

Investigation [Intelligence] (Charisma)

Nature [Intelligence] (Wisdom)

Religion [Intelligence] (Wisdom)

Animal Handling [Wisdom] (Intelligence) (Charisma)

Insight [Wisdom] (Charisma)

Medicine [Wisdom] (Intelligence)

Perception [Wisdom]

Survival [Wisdom] (Intelligence)

Deception [Charisma] (Wisdom)

Intimidation [Charisma] (Strength) (Constitution)

Performance [Charisma] (Dexterity) (Intelligence) (Wisdom)

Persuasion [Charisma] (Intelligence)

EDIT: I also add what I call "Scaling Skill Checks", which allows excessively high rolls to be rewarded.

For example: A task (like opening a trapped, locked chest) has a DC of 15 to open, followed by a dexterity save against the trap.

Rolling 1-4 under the DC (11-14) causes you to force open the lock, making lots of noise and giving you disadvantage on the save vs the trap.

Rolling 0-4 over the DC (15-19) causes you to unlock it with no issues, but the trap springs. Roll normally to save.

Rolling 5-9 over (20-24) gives you advantage on the save, since you saw the trap was there.

Rolling 10+ over (25+) means you disarmed the trap, and now you can keep whatever it was to use for your own devices.

Should you need to roll to save vs. the trap, I would add relevant skill bonuses. In this case, add your total perception bonus to your dexterity saving throw.

With this kind of system, you can have low DCs for your average player, but still reward your skill monkey Bards and Rogues for having massive skill bonuses compared to everyone else.

Dual Wielding is super-weak late game (Can only be used with Light Weapons without a feat, does not use your mod for the second attack without fighting style, replaces your bonus action for an offhand attack. Means nothing when you strike 4 times with one weapon (4d6+20) just to use your bonus action for an unmodified 1d6).

So I modified it so that an offhand attack is considered part of your attack action rather than consuming a bonus action. So a Ranger could cast Hunter's Mark (bonus action) and then strike you with his two shortswords in the same turn, which puts non-two handed melee damage as a valid option.

The goliath's (Unearthed Arcana: Elemental Evil) Stone Endurance is too strong at early levels but has little scaling for later levels. The d12 is also fairly unreliable for a one-shot power.

I changed it to 1d6 + Con mod + prof. bonus. At level 1, this makes it about a 7-12 roll (as opposed to 5-16). At 20, this will become a 12-17 (as opposed to 6-17).

When players' flaws and traits can be interpreted in combat, I will give buffs and debuffs to them to give them a sort of uniqueness.

For example, I had this girl playing a Ranger who felt more comfortable with animals than she did people. So I dropped her charisma by 2 and gave her expertise on Animal Handling.

Totemic Barbarians, when they use their Spirit Walker feature (uses Commune with Nature as a ritual at level 10), they can replace one of their animal spirits options with a different spirit, or replace all three options with the same animal.

Modifying more than one specific slot requires additional ritual castings of the spell.
